claim: Ischemic stroke accounts for 87% of all strokes.
source: Ischemic stroke, which accounts for 87% of all strokes, is the second most common cause of death and the leading cause of acquired disability in adults worldwide (Brott and Bogousslavsky, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brott and Bogousslavsky, 2000

claim: Ischemic stroke is the second most common cause of death worldwide.
source: Ischemic stroke, which accounts for 87% of all strokes, is the second most common cause of death and the leading cause of acquired disability in adults worldwide (Brott and Bogousslavsky, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brott and Bogousslavsky, 2000

claim: Ischemic stroke is the leading cause of acquired disability in adults worldwide.
source: Ischemic stroke, which accounts for 87% of all strokes, is the second most common cause of death and the leading cause of acquired disability in adults worldwide (Brott and Bogousslavsky, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brott and Bogousslavsky, 2000

claim: Current therapy for ischemic stroke represented by rapid circulation restoration only benefits approximately 5% of patients.
source: However, current therapy represented by rapid circulation restoration only benefits ~5% of patients due to the narrow treatment window and small vessel blockage (Brott and Bogousslavsky, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brott and Bogousslavsky, 2000

claim: The narrow treatment window and small vessel blockage limit the effectiveness of current stroke therapy.
source: However, current therapy represented by rapid circulation restoration only benefits ~5% of patients due to the narrow treatment window and small vessel blockage (Brott and Bogousslavsky, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brott and Bogousslavsky, 2000

claim: Epigenetic alterations play important roles in the pathogenesis of stroke.

evidence: Supported by citation to Stanzione et al., 2020

claim: Global DNA methylation, histone methylation, histone acetylation, microRNAs, enhancer RNAs, and circular RNAs show significant changes after cerebral ischemia in animal models or human patients.
source: For example, global DNA methylation, histone methylation, histone acetylation, microRNAs, enhancer RNAs, and circular RNAs were found to show significant changes after cerebral ischemia in animal models or human patients (Stanzione et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stanzione et al., 2020

claim: Inhibition of DNA methyltransferases or histone deacetylases by genetic or chemical mechanisms protects against stroke-induced brain damage.
source: Furthermore, inhibition of DNA methyltransferases or histone deacetylases by genetic or chemical mechanisms was shown to protect against stroke-induced brain damage (Zhao et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2016

claim: Polycomb repressive complex genes play important roles in neuroprotection after stroke.
source: Polycomb repressive complex genes were found to play important roles in neuroprotection after stroke (Kuehner and Yao, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kuehner and Yao, 2019

claim: Middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) in rodents can produce reliable and well-reproducible infarcts.
source: In vivo, middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) in rodents can produce reliable and well-reproducible infarcts and became a commonly used approach to mimic human ischemic stroke.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about MCAO models

claim: MCAO is a commonly used approach to mimic human ischemic stroke.
source: In vivo, middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) in rodents can produce reliable and well-reproducible infarcts and became a commonly used approach to mimic human ischemic stroke.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about MCAO models

claim: Oxygen-glucose deprivation (OGD) treatment has been widely used to examine the cellular mechanisms involved in cerebral ischemia.
source: For example, oxygen-glucose deprivation (OGD) treatment has been widely used to examine the cellular mechanisms involved in cerebral ischemia and identify potential neuroprotective agents and pathways (Bernstock et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bernstock et al., 2016

claim: An RNAi screen was carried out on epigenetic regulators using the OGD model in HT-22 cells.
source: In this study, we used the OGD model in the immortalized mouse hippocampal neuronal cell line HT-22 and carried out an RNAi screen on epigenetic regulators.
evidence: Description of the experimental approach used in the study

claim: PRMT5 was identified as a novel negative regulator of neuronal cell survival after OGD.
source: We identified PRMT5 as a novel negative regulator of neuronal cell survival after OGD.
evidence: Based on the results of the RNAi screen described in the study

claim: PRMT5 translocates from the cytosol to the nucleus upon oxygen and energy depletion both in vitro and in vivo.
source: PRMT5 was identified as a novel negative regulator of neuronal cell survival after OGD, which presented a phenotype of translocation from the cytosol to the nucleus upon oxygen and energy depletion both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figures 2 and 3

claim: PRMT5 binds to chromatin and a large number of promoter regions to repress downstream gene expression.
source: PRMT5 bound to the chromatin and a large number of promoter regions to repress downstream gene expression.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data presented in the study

claim: Silencing Prmt5 significantly dampened the OGD-induced changes for a large-scale of genes.
source: Silencing Prmt5 significantly dampened the OGD-induced changes for a large-scale of genes, and gene ontology analysis showed that PRMT5-target genes were highly enriched for Hedgehog signaling.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data presented in the study

claim: PRMT5-target genes are highly enriched for Hedgehog signaling.
source: Silencing Prmt5 significantly dampened the OGD-induced changes for a large-scale of genes, and gene ontology analysis showed that PRMT5-target genes were highly enriched for Hedgehog signaling.
evidence: Supported by gene ontology analysis of RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data

claim: PRMT5 inhibition with EPZ015666 sustains protection against neuronal death in vivo in mice treated with middle cerebral artery occlusion.
source: Encouraged by the above observation, mice were treated with middle cerebral artery occlusion with the PRMT5 inhibitor EPZ015666 and found that PRMT5 inhibition sustains protection against neuronal death in vivo.
evidence: Supported by in vivo experimental data in MCAO mouse model

claim: 8 hours of oxygen and glucose deprivation followed by 24 hours of normal culture caused significant cell death with a small but consistent percentage of surviving cells in HT-22 cells.
source: We chose 8 hr of oxygen and glucose deprivation followed by 24 hr of normal culture for the screen because it caused significant amount of cell death with small but consistent percentage of surviving cells.
evidence: Based on optimization experiments for the OGD protocol

claim: 125 genes involved in epigenetic and chromatin regulation were selected for the shRNA library.
source: Next, we selected 125 genes involved in epigenetic and chromatin regulation and generated an shRNA library targeting these genes in the pLKO.1 vector (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Description of the experimental design

claim: Most shRNAs were depleted after OGD treatment, suggesting that the genes they target are likely required for cell survival during or after OGD.
source: Based on the representation of the shRNAs in the cells, we found that most of the shRNAs were depleted after OGD treatment, suggesting that the genes they target are likely required for cell survival during or after OGD.
evidence: Based on sequencing data from the RNAi screen

claim: A small number of shRNAs showed increased representations after OGD, suggesting that inhibition of their target genes likely promoted cell survival.
source: Importantly, we also found a small number of shRNAs that showed increased representations after OGD, suggesting that the inhibition of their target genes likely promoted cell survival.
evidence: Based on sequencing data from the RNAi screen

claim: shRNAs against Dnmt3b, Pcgf6, and Mga were enriched after OGD treatment.
source: Encouragingly, shRNAs against Dnmt3b, Pcgf6, and Mga were among those that are enriched after OGD treatment (Figure 1B), consistent with the notion that DNA methylation and polycomb repressive complexes play important roles in stroke injury and neuroprotection (Endres et al., 2000; Dock et al., 2015; Elder et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by screen data shown in Figure 1B and citations

claim: DNA methylation and polycomb repressive complexes play important roles in stroke injury and neuroprotection.
source: Encouragingly, shRNAs against Dnmt3b, Pcgf6, and Mga were among those that are enriched after OGD treatment (Figure 1B), consistent with the notion that DNA methylation and polycomb repressive complexes play important roles in stroke injury and neuroprotection (Endres et al., 2000; Dock et al., 2015; Elder et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Endres et al., 2000; Dock et al., 2015; Elder et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2019

claim: The shRNA against Prmt5 displayed the largest fold change among enriched shRNAs.
source: Among the enriched shRNAs, the shRNA against Prmt5 displayed the largest fold change (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by screen data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Prmt5 knockdown by the original pLKO.1 shRNA and two new pGIPZ shRNAs all led to significant improvement in HT-22 cell survival after OGD.
source: We found that Prmt5 knockdown (KD) by the original pLKO.1 shRNA as well as the two new pGIPZ shRNAs all led to significant improvement in HT-22 cell survival after OGD (Figure 1C).

claim: Treatment of HT-22 cells with the PRMT5 inhibitor EPZ015666 resulted in improved cell survival after OGD.
source: Moreover, treatment of the cells with a small-molecule PRMT5 inhibitor EPZ015666 resulted in similar outcomes (Figure 1D), further supporting the fact that PRMT5 is responsible for the protective effect.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: PRMT5 inhibition significantly reduced OGD-induced HT-22 cell death in the lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) cytotoxicity assay.
source: Consistent with the above results based on cell numbers, PRMT5 inhibition significantly reduced OGD-induced HT-22 cell death in the lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) cytotoxicity assay (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E

claim: Prmt5 shRNA or PRMT5 inhibitor promoted the survival of primary mouse neurons in culture after OGD treatment.
source: Finally, in addition to the immortalized HT-22 cell line, Prmt5 shRNA or PRMT5 inhibitor promoted the survival of primary mouse neurons in culture after OGD treatment (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1D-E

claim: PRMT5 is predominantly localized in the cytoplasm under normal conditions in HT-22 cells.
source: It was found that PRMT5 is predominantly localized in the cytoplasm under normal conditions.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging data

claim: Upon OGD treatment, PRMT5 relocates to the nucleus and becomes enriched in the nuclear compartment in HT-22 cells.
source: Upon OGD treatment, however, it relocates to the nucleus and becomes enriched in the nuclear compartment (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Endogenous HA-tagged PRMT5 translocates from the cytosol to the nucleus after OGD in HT-22 cells.
source: Similarly, we found that the endogenous HA-tagged PRMT5 translocates from the cytosol to the nucleus after OGD (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging data using HA antibody shown in Figure 2A

claim: PRMT5 protein moved from the cytoplasm to the nucleus in OGD-treated HT-22 cells based on biochemical fractionation.
source: Consistent with the above, PRMT5 protein moved from the cytoplasm to the nucleus in OGD-treated cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by biochemical fractionation data shown in Figure 2B

claim: PRMT5 protein became largely chromatin-bound after OGD treatment in HT-22 cells.
source: Further, we found that PRMT5 protein became largely chromatin-bound, suggesting that it may participate in OGD-induced transcriptional responses.
evidence: Supported by biochemical fractionation data

claim: PRMT5 nuclear translocation was observed in OGD-treated primary mouse neurons in culture.
source: Finally, we repeated the experiments in OGD-treated primary mouse neurons in culture and observed the same result (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2C and D

claim: PRMT5 signal was mostly detected in the cytoplasm on the contralateral side of MCAO-treated mouse brain.
source: Similar to what was observed in cultured cells, PRMT5 signal was mostly detected in the cytoplasm on the contralateral side, but became highly enriched in the nucleus on the ipsilateral side (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3A

claim: PRMT5 became highly enriched in the nucleus on the ipsilateral side of MCAO-treated mouse brain.
source: Similar to what was observed in cultured cells, PRMT5 signal was mostly detected in the cytoplasm on the contralateral side, but became highly enriched in the nucleus on the ipsilateral side (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3A

claim: PRMT5 nuclear translocation was detected in both the penumbra area and ischemic core of the ipsilateral side after MCAO.
source: Upon closer examination, PRMT5 nuclear translocation was detected in both the penumbra area and ischemic core of the ipsilateral side (Figure 3B).

claim: PRMT5 translocates into the nucleus and binds to the chromatin upon ischemic injury in neuronal tissues based on biochemical fractionation.
source: Importantly, biochemical fractionation of the neuronal tissues again showed that PRMT5 not only translocates into the nucleus but also binds to the chromatin upon ischemic injury (Figure 3D).

claim: OGD treatment led to the upregulation of 2186 genes and downregulation of 2926 genes in HT-22 cells.
source: We found that OGD treatment led to the upregulation of 2186 genes and downregulation of 2926 genes (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 2).

claim: Prmt5 knockdown alone had minimal impact on gene expression in HT-22 cells.
source: Interestingly, while Prmt5 KD alone had minimal impact on gene expression, it significantly dampened the OGD-induced changes for a large number of genes (Figure 4B, Supplementary file 2).

claim: 1035 of the 2186 OGD-induced genes were reversed or partially reversed upon Prmt5 knockdown.
source: Specifically, 1035 of the 2186 OGD-induced genes and 2090 of the 2926 OGD-repressed genes were reversed or partially reversed upon Prmt5 KD (Figure 4B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B

claim: 2090 of the 2926 OGD-repressed genes were reversed or partially reversed upon Prmt5 knockdown.
source: Specifically, 1035 of the 2186 OGD-induced genes and 2090 of the 2926 OGD-repressed genes were reversed or partially reversed upon Prmt5 KD (Figure 4B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B

claim: 16,061 peaks were identified as bound by PRMT5 in OGD-treated HT-22 cells by ChIP-seq.
source: In total, we identified 16,061 peaks bound by PRMT5.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data

claim: 56% of PRMT5-bound genomic regions are near the transcription start sites (TSSs).
source: Interestingly, a significant fraction of the PRMT5-bound genomic regions (56%) are near the transcription start sites (TSSs) (Figure 4C, Supplementary file 2), consistent with the notion that PRMT5 may regulate downstream gene expression.

claim: PRMT5 occupies the promoter regions of a large fraction of the 2090 genes that were down-reversed genes in OGD.
source: Indeed, when intercepted with the RNA-seq data, we found that PRMT5 occupies the promoter regions of a large fraction of the 2090 genes that were down-reversed genes in OGD (Figure 4D, Supplementary file 2).

claim: OGD-repressed genes are dependent on PRMT5 as Prmt5 knockdown largely reversed their expression changes in OGD.

claim: Under OGD conditions PRMT5 enters the nucleus and suppresses the expression of its target genes.
source: Therefore, we defined these genes that are bound by PRMT5, downregulated after OGD treatment but rescued by Prmt5 KD as PRMT5-target genes in OGD. And the above results suggested that under OGD conditions PRMT5 enters the nucleus and suppresses the expression of its target genes.

claim: PRMT5 occupied the promoter regions of Ptch1 and Smo.

claim: PRMT5 is responsible for the downregulation of Ptch1 and Smo after OGD treatment.
source: It was found that PRMT5 indeed occupied their promoter regions (Figure 4G and H) and is responsible for their downregulation after OGD treatment (Figure 4I).

claim: Upon oxygen and glucose deprivation, PRMT5 promotes neuronal cell death by repressing the expression of genes involved in Hedgehog signaling.
source: Together, our findings strongly supported the notion that upon oxygen and glucose deprivation, PRMT5 promotes neuronal cell death by repressing the expression of genes involved in Hedgehog signaling.

claim: Prmt5 silencing provides neuroprotection by preventing the inhibition of Hedgehog pathways.
source: Prmt5 silencing provides neuroprotection by preventing the inhibition of Hedgehog pathways.
evidence: Based on integration of multiple experimental results

claim: PRMT5-target genes in OGD are highly enriched for those that were downregulated after cerebral infarction in the MCAO mouse model.
source: We found that PRMT5-target genes in OGD are highly enriched for those that were downregulated after cerebral infarction in the MCAO mouse (Figure 5A), suggesting that our model may apply in animals.

claim: PRMT5 inhibition with EPZ015666 reduced the infarct volume after MCAO in mice.

claim: PRMT5 inhibition with EPZ015666 increased the number of NeuN-positive neurons after MCAO in mice.
source: Indeed, we found that PRMT5 inhibition resulted in significant protective effects. Specifically, EPZ015666 treatment reduced the infarct volume (Figure 5B) and increased the number of NeuN-positive neurons after MCAO (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: PRMT5 inhibition with EPZ015666 reduced the water content and tissue swelling caused by infarction after MCAO in mice.
source: It also reduced the water content and tissue swelling caused by infarction (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D

claim: EPZ015666 treatment led to significantly improved functional recovery in animals as evidenced by the reduction in the neurological deficit scores after MCAO.
source: Most importantly, we found that EPZ015666 treatment led to significantly improved functional recovery in the animals as evidenced by the reduction in the neurological deficit scores (Figure 5E).

claim: PRMT5 plays a critical role in mediating neuronal cell death after ischemic injury in the brain.

claim: PRMT5 may serve as a novel therapeutic target for stroke treatment.
